title: The Mule
attribution: Excerpted verbatim from Aesop's Fables, translated by V. S. Vernon Jones (1912), via Project Gutenberg.
body: One morning a Mule, who had too much to eat and too little to do, began to think himself a very fine fellow indeed, and frisked about saying, "My father was undoubtedly a high-spirited horse and I take after him entirely." But very soon afterwards he was put into the harness and compelled to go a very long way with a heavy load behind him. At the end of the day, exhausted by his unusual exertions, he said dejectedly to himself, "I must have been mistaken about my father; he can only have been an ass after all."

questions.prompt: According to the passage, what condition led the Mule to think himself a very fine fellow?
options: He had too much to eat and too little to do
He had just won a race against a horse
He had been praised by his master that morning
He had grown much larger than the other mules

questions.prompt: According to the passage, what did the Mule do while thinking so highly of himself?
options: Frisked about
Refused to eat
Challenged a horse to a race
Hid from his master

questions.prompt: According to the passage, what does the Mule claim about his father?
options: That he was undoubtedly a high-spirited horse
That he was the fastest mule ever known
That he had once pulled a king's carriage
That he had taught him everything he knew

questions.prompt: According to the passage, what happened to the Mule soon after he made his boast?
options: He was put into the harness and made to pull a heavy load a long way
He was sold to a passing merchant
He was given an even lighter workload
He was praised by his master for his fine appearance

questions.prompt: According to the passage, how did the Mule feel at the end of the day?
options: Exhausted by his unusual exertions
Refreshed after a good rest
Proud of how far he had traveled
Angry at his master for overworking him

questions.prompt: According to the passage, what does the Mule finally decide his father must have been?
options: An ass
A horse after all
Neither a horse nor an ass
A mule just like himself

questions.prompt: Based on the passage, why does the Mule change his mind about his father after the day's hard labor?
options: His exhausting workload reminds him of a burden-bearing ass rather than a spirited horse
He overhears his master discussing his true parentage
He meets a horse who tells him the truth about his father
He realizes horses are never put into harnesses at all

questions.prompt: Which statement best captures the point of the fable?
options: Good fortune can inflate one's sense of self, but hardship quickly reveals a truer picture
Mules are always stronger workers than horses
It is wrong to ever boast about one's family
Hard labor always improves an animal's character

questions.prompt: According to the passage, when did the Mule begin to think so highly of himself?
options: One morning
After a long journey
Following a heavy meal at night
Just before harvest season

questions.prompt: According to the passage, what kind of load was the Mule compelled to pull?
options: A heavy load
An empty cart
A load of feathers
No load at all, only the harness itself

questions.prompt: According to the passage, how does the Mule speak to himself at the end of the day?
options: Dejectedly
Cheerfully
Angrily at his master
Proudly

questions.prompt: Based on the passage, what does the Mule's shifting claims about his father suggest about how he judges himself?
options: He bases his sense of identity on his current circumstances rather than any real knowledge of his parentage
He has always known for certain which parent he takes after
He values his mother's lineage more than his father's
He believes mules are inherently superior to both horses and asses

questions.prompt: As the passage uses it, what does "exertions" mean in "exhausted by his unusual exertions"?
options: Strenuous efforts or physical labor
Long periods of rest
Sudden bursts of anger
Careful, quiet thoughts

questions.prompt: Which of these best summarizes what happens in the passage?
options: A well-fed, idle Mule boasts of horse-like ancestry, but after a day of hard labor concludes his father must have been an ass instead
A Mule proves his horse ancestry by outrunning every other animal on the farm
A Mule refuses to work and is punished by his master for laziness
A Mule and a horse compete to see who can pull the heavier load
